children.text: The largest of the seven crater lakes behind San Pablo City Hall in Laguna, with a roughly 3.7 km lakeside promenade that lets you walk past Mount Banahaw views and tilapia fish pens. It is free to enter and easy to visit from Manila in half a day.
Lake Sampaloc is a crater lake in the heart of San Pablo City, Laguna, about

southeast of Manila. The lake lies right behind City Hall, so you can reach it on foot from downtown with no gate or ticket booth, which sets it apart from the other lakes. San Pablo has seven volcanic lakes scattered around it (Sampaloc, Palakpakin, Calibato, Mohicap, Bunot, Yambo, and Pandin) and is known as the "City of Seven Lakes"; Sampaloc is the largest and the most visited.
The lake covers about
104 hectares
, is up to about
1.2 km
wide, and is about
deep at its deepest (about

on average). It is a "maar," a crater lake that formed when groundwater met hot magma and exploded, leaving a collapsed hollow that filled with water, and it is one of the small volcanoes scattered across the volcanic zone between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw. A paved path of about
3.7 km
circles the shore, and on a clear day the ridge of Mount Banahaw rises across the water.

A local legend tells the story. A stingy old woman had a giant sampaloc (tamarind) tree in her garden, and when she refused to give a passing old beggar even one fruit, the beggar revealed himself as a fairy (diwata); at that moment the whole orchard sank into an enormous pit that filled with water. That is how the lake got its name, "Sampaloc," the Tagalog word for tamarind.

For the people who live here, the lake is a livelihood before it is a view. Tilapia farming took hold in the mid-1950s, so bamboo fish cages and floating huts dot the water, and a big tilapia statue stands on the lakeside road to mark it. It suits families, couples, and photographers who want to stroll for an hour or two, snack at the roadside stalls, and use it as the starting point for a seven-lakes trip. It is not a place for swimming or adventure activities.
The loop around the lake is about
3.7 km
, and at a slow pace it takes around
1 hour
. It is paved and mostly flat, so it is manageable even with children. Joggers fill it in the early morning and families stroll it at dusk, giving it the buzz of a city lake.
Mount Banahaw rises across the lake at about
above sea level. Come around
6–7 AM
, before the clouds sink low, and the outline of the mountain is clear while light spreads across the water. In rainy months the mountain is often hidden behind cloud.
Bicycles and e-bikes can be rented at the lakeside, so if walking feels like too much, you can circle the lake in about
20–30 minutes
. Visitors' reviews put e-bikes from around
, but check the rate and rental time on the spot.

blocks.title: A viewing deck above the lake

children.text: A viewing deck with a white balustrade stands on high ground by the lake, giving a sweeping view of the whole lake and the mountain slopes beyond. A signboard introduces the seven lakes, so it is a good place to understand how San Pablo's lakes formed before you start.
A large tilapia statue stands on the lakeside road, and the plaque beside it records that on
April 16, 1955

, during the term of Mayor Tomas Dizon, Mr. and Mrs. Jose Agahan donated the first tilapia fingerlings to Lakes Sampaloc and Palakpakin. It is a symbol of how San Pablo became a city that lives off lake aquaculture.

Huts built on bamboo rafts and net fish cages float on the lake. From the shore you can watch fishermen paddle narrow dugout boats between the cages, feeding the fish and checking the nets. Ask permission before taking photos of fishermen and their work areas.

blocks.title: The Marian shrine on the lakeshore

children.text: Beside the lakeside road there is a small grotto shrine of stacked stone, with a statue of the Virgin Mary facing the lake and local people praying. It is a quiet resting spot that shows how Catholic faith is woven into daily life in a Philippine city.

Stalls selling drinks and snacks line the road next to the promenade. The most common way to enjoy the lake is to buy coconut juice, corn with shaved ice (mais con yelo), or a grilled snack and sit on a bench looking at the water. At the lakeside restaurants you can try tilapia cooked from the lake.
Start at the promenade entrance and take in the morning view from the side where Mount Banahaw is visible

Visiting all seven lakes needs a chartered tricycle and more than one day. Pick just one or two, such as Sampaloc and Pandin, or Bunot or Calibato.
Take a Lucena-bound bus (DLTB, JAC Liner, JAM Liner) from the Cubao, Pasay Buendia, or Parañaque PITX terminals in Manila. Buses usually run about every hour, the ride takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes
, and the one-way fare is about

The bus drops you at SM City San Pablo on the Maharlika Highway. Tell the conductor "San Pablo" in advance. Early-morning departures are fastest, and Manila-bound buses are crowded on weekend afternoons.
From the stop, take a tricycle to the lake. The fare is about
, and a group of four can split the cost of one tricycle.
From Manila take the SLEX, leave at the Calamba exit, and follow the Maharlika Highway (Pan-Philippine Highway) through Los Baños into San Pablo. The distance is about
, and the drive takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
when traffic is light but can run over
2 hours 30 minutes
on weekends.
Enter "San Pablo City Hall" in your map app and you will arrive right behind it. There is parking along the lakeside promenade, but spaces run short on weekends.

The Philippine National Railways (PNR) southern line once linked Calamba, San Pablo, and Lucena, but its routes and timetables change often. If you plan to go by train, check the latest PNR announcements before you leave, and take the bus if you want a sure way to get there.
From downtown to the lake it is about
by tricycle, and since the lake is right behind City Hall, you can also walk from the town center.
You can walk the promenade once around (about
1 hour
) or rent a bicycle.
To reach the other lakes, it is easier to charter a tricycle for about half a day. An old article put a tricycle charter around all seven lakes at about
, so agree on the current price with the driver first.
The dry season in southern Laguna runs
December–May
December–February
is especially good for walking, with cool mornings and evenings and little rain, and clear days make Mount Banahaw stand out sharply. In
March–May
the midday temperature can reach
, so it is better to walk the lakeshore, which has little shade, early in the morning or at dusk.
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and typhoons can pass over southern Luzon from
July–October
. When it rains the mountain hides behind cloud and the lake loses some of its charm, but there are fewer people. The best hours are around
6–8 AM
and
. San Pablo's Coconut Festival is to be held on the city's cityhood anniversary,
May 7
, from
, so check the city's tourism notices for the schedule. Fish kills have occurred at the lake in sudden weather changes, as in
January 2021
at the start of the dry season, so some days the fish-farm areas can look messy.

Most people visit from Manila as a day trip, but if you want to walk the lake early in the morning or link the seven lakes and nearby sights, staying in downtown San Pablo is convenient. Downtown has mid-range hotels, B&Bs, and guesthouses at about
per night. Choosing one within walking distance of the lake makes an early-morning stroll easy. Rooms fill up quickly on weekends and in Holy Week, so book ahead.

Tilapia raised in the lake is the signature food by the lakeshore. Restaurants along the lake serve grilled and fried tilapia with rice. The stalls next to the promenade sell coconut juice, corn with shaved ice, and grilled snacks, and in downtown San Pablo you can often find lomi, a thick noodle soup. As a coconut-growing area, San Pablo has many sweets and drinks made with coconut, and on the way back it is a good place to pick up Laguna's famous buko pie, kesong puti (white cheese), and espasol (a coconut-dusted rice cake). Because of the water quality in the lake, avoid raw fish dishes and eat food that is cooked through.
There is no admission fee, so you can fit it into your route freely. For restrooms, it is better to use City Hall or a lakeside restaurant.
The best times are
6–8 AM
and
. At midday there is little shade, and walking in
heat is hard.
Bring a hat, sunscreen, and a bottle of water. You can buy water at the lakeside stalls and shops.
When renting a bicycle, ask about the rate and return time first and check the brakes and tires. The lakeside is busy with pedestrians, so ride slowly.
The Pandin raft tour often requires a minimum of 4 people, so if your group is small, contact the village cooperative in advance to ask whether you can join another group.
Check the last bus back to Manila ahead of time. Manila-bound buses run frequently, but they are crowded and the roads are jammed on Sunday evenings, so confirm the last departure with the operator.
Bring plenty of cash. Street stalls, tricycles, and small restaurants mostly take cash only. It is easiest to withdraw it beforehand at SM City San Pablo or a bank downtown.
Ask permission before photographing fishermen and fish-farm workers. The huts on the lake are often privately owned, so do not climb onto them.

The water quality of Lake Sampaloc is poor because of fish feed and household wastewater, and even reports from the Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA) are known to show ammonia and phosphate levels above the standards. Do not swim in the lake or drink its water. This is a place for walking and looking, not a lake for water play.
When oxygen in the water drops sharply because the fish farms are crowded, fish die all at once in what is called a fish kill. In
January 2021
about 2 tons of tilapia were lost. On such days the lakeshore can smell, so postpone your visit or keep it short.
Pedestrians, bicycles, and motorbikes share the promenade. It gets crowded on weekend evenings, so keep hold of children's hands and be especially careful near the railing on the lake side.
Watch out for pickpockets, as in any place where crowds gather. Carry your bag in front and keep valuables out of sight.

In the rainy season the paths are wet and slippery, and heavy rain can flood low parts of the lakeside. If a typhoon warning is issued, postpone your visit and check the local government's latest notices.
The fish cages and floating huts on the lake are the residents' livelihood. Do not throw trash into the lake, and do not approach the fish-farm nets or boats without permission.
